PC ports lack an accepted standard for what constitutes "done". In many case, the standard is simply, "We got it to run on PC, it's done." Any time we come across a port that is "broken and unplayable" on PC for a large number of gamers, there is still always an element that are able to run it without issue. The vast array of hardware configurations that are encountered from one PC to the next makes for a very different development requirement compared to consoles which all have practically identical inner components from one unit to the next.

A pet peeve of mine that illustrates the nature of the conversions to get a game that works on one or more types of console to getting it to work on PC is the "...please do not turn off your system while you see this icon..." notices. Those are relevant to consoles. No PC users with any sense at all turns off their PC from the power switch while a game is running unless the game has crashed and hard locked the machine. Simply changing that text string to "Saving in progress..." would lend an element of polish to any port. Why isn't it done? Because porting isn't seen as an investment that reflects on the branding of the game. It's seen as a necessary step to access an additional market. As long as developers and, more importantly, publishers, treat it like a necessary evil, the quality of ports to PC will always be highly inconsistent.

One thing about consoles is that developers have to fine tune everything to make sure it runs at the target framerate. The developers actually have something to aim for. This is why we get these beautiful games that run well on the limited hardware of a single console. An exclusive title. Nintendo understands this an is able to develop hardware that fits their games like a glove. Since they are developing hardware to find their games rather than developing games as a makeshift for whatever hardware they have to develop for, their consoles end up underpowered when it comes to third party titles they didn't have in mind when creating the hardware. Back to Sony and Microsoft, they take parts they can throw together to make the console run whatever games are thrown at it. This is more third-party friendly as the developers don't have to work around and learn the quirks of special rendering techniques that Nintendo made for their games. The advantage developers also have is that they know exactly how smoothly the game runs, so they work around it. On PC the dev has no idea how well to optimize the game due to all the different configurations of billions of PC cpu-gpu-ram combinations. Because the developer has nowhere to aim, we get bad PC ports. The developer has to choose a target somewhere, and since they already targeted console hardware, they just bring it straight over without thorough testing. At the end of the day, PC is not a master race, and developers who know exactly what framerate they'll get will make a game that takes better advantage of the hardware. If developers have control of the hardware and have a deep understanding of it is when we get the most beautiful, most well optimized games. Just look at twilight princess on the GameCube, that was amazing, same goes for flower for ps3. It's kind of sad that consoles have gone to x86 as consoles were where all the graphical innovation could happen. Consoles need to stop trying to be PCs and just dedicate themselves to making great looking games, multiplatform gaming is in a way killing the console. Graphics is a lot more than just pushing more polygons per second.
